# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 35 (Bu-Vb Pc35)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc35
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 35
**Title (English, from literature):** Eating more after refusing an invitation
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 35 (entitled *Pavāraṇā*) governs the monastic offence incurred when a Buddhist monk eats additional food after having concluded his meal and refused further offerings [Hüsken 1997]. Under the rule, a monk who has eaten and formally indicated that he is satisfied (*pavārito*) incurs an offence of expiation (*pācittiya*) if he consumes solid or soft food that is not monastic leftovers (*anatiritta*) [Hüsken 1997; Entrance to the Vinaya 1983]. In the canonical word commentary (*padabhājana*), the condition of having eaten (*bhuttāvī*) is defined as consuming even an amount of the five staple foods as small as what clings to the tip of a grass blade, while being "satisfied" (*pavārito*) is defined by the physical offering of food within arm's reach that is declined [Hüsken 1997]. The commentary (*Samantapāsādikā*, Sp 821) notes that the Pali bhikkhu rule specifically adds the exemption clause *anatiritta* ("not left over"), which differentiates it from the corresponding bhikkhunī rule [Hüsken 1997].

In early Buddhist monastic history and doctrinal literature, Pācittiya 35 is closely connected to the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of *khalupacchābhattikaṅga* (refusing food offered after completing one's meal) [Dutt 1941]. It also features prominently in canonical and historical accounts of the Second Buddhist Council: several of the ten controversial lax practices attributed to the Vaisālī monks—particularly *gāmantarakappa* (walking to a second village to take another meal) and *amathitakappa* (consuming unchurned milk or buttermilk after mealtime)—were judged to contravene Pācittiya 35 [Bapat 1956; Sarao and Long 2017; Dutt 1978; Entrance to the Vinaya 1983].

Parallels to this training rule exist in the Prātimokṣa and Vibhaṅga texts of all surviving Vinaya traditions, including the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, and Mahāsaṅghika recensions preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan, alongside the parallel nuns' rules. DharmaNexus confirms substantial text reuse within the Pali canon, notably sharing extensive formulaic text with the bhikkhunī parallel Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 54 (§0.4–1.20 ↔ §0.4–1.19 at 93% similarity), neighboring food rules in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (such as Pācittiya 36, 33, 32, and 31, and Pāṭidesanīya rules 1, 3, and 4), the Khandhakas (Kd 11 and Kd 6), and post-canonical Vinaya handbooks (*Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā* and *Vinayavinicchayaṭīkā*) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages with the Tibetan *Vinaya-uttaragrantha* and the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi* [DharmaNexus].
